
# How to Connect External Speakers or a Soundbar to Your TV


## What is this in plain English?


Think back to televisions from the 1970s and 80s—those big, heavy cabinet TVs with speakers built right into the front of the wooden console. The speakers were large, faced toward you, and the sound filled the room. You could hear every word clearly because the TV was designed with audio quality in mind.


Modern flat-screen TVs are the opposite. They're thin, sleek, and beautiful to look at, but manufacturers sacrificed sound quality to achieve that slim design. The speakers are tiny—sometimes no bigger than a matchbook—and they're usually hidden on the back or bottom of the TV, firing sound toward the wall or floor instead of toward you. It's like trying to listen to music through a transistor radio when you're used to a proper stereo system.


This is where external speakers and soundbars come in. A soundbar is essentially a long, thin speaker that sits below or above your TV and contains multiple speaker drivers in one sleek unit—think of it as a complete speaker system compressed into a single bar. External speakers can range from a simple pair of bookshelf speakers to a full surround sound system with speakers positioned around your room. Both options dramatically improve your TV's sound quality, making dialogue clearer, music richer, and action scenes more immersive.


Connecting these speakers to your TV isn't complicated—you're essentially just plugging cables into the right ports—but it can feel overwhelming if you're not familiar with the different types of connections (HDMI, optical, RCA, etc.). This guide will walk you through everything step-by-step, in plain language, so you can enjoy the clear, powerful sound your favorite shows and movies deserve.


## Before You Start: Understanding Why You Need Better Speakers


**The Problem with Modern TV Speakers:**


**Why built-in TV speakers are inadequate:**


**1. Size limitations:**

- Flat-screen TVs are 2-3 inches thick
- Speakers must fit in that tiny space
- Physics: larger speakers = better sound
- Tiny speakers = tinny, weak sound
- No room for bass (low frequency sounds)

**2. Poor positioning:**

- **Downward-firing:** Speakers point at your TV stand, sound bounces off furniture
- **Rear-firing:** Speakers point at the wall behind TV, sound reflects back muddy and unclear
- **Side-firing:** Better than down/rear, but still not optimal
- **Almost never front-firing** (toward you, like old TVs)

**3. Insufficient power:**

- Built-in speakers: 10-20 watts total
- External speakers: 100-300+ watts
- More power = louder, clearer sound
- Better for larger rooms

**4. No separation:**

- Stereo sound requires left and right speakers separated
- TV speakers are 12-36 inches apart
- Not enough separation for true stereo effect
- External speakers can be positioned optimally

**Real-world consequences:**


**You've probably experienced:**

- Can't hear dialogue clearly (constantly adjusting volume)
- Explosions and music are loud, but talking is muffled
- Turning volume up to hear dialogue, then commercials blast you
- Sound lacks depth and richness
- Hard to understand accents or whispered lines
- Missing subtle sound effects that enhance the experience

**What External Speakers Fix:**


**Soundbar benefits:**

- Larger speaker drivers (better sound quality)
- Multiple speakers in one unit (left, right, center channels)
- Front-facing (sound projects toward you)
- Dialogue enhancement modes (specifically boost speech frequencies)
- More power (louder without distortion)
- Better bass response (or includes separate subwoofer)
- Takes up minimal space

**Full speaker system benefits:**

- True stereo separation (speakers positioned around room)
- Dedicated center channel (just for dialogue)
- Surround sound (audio from all directions)
- Subwoofer for deep bass
- Cinema-quality experience
- Scalable (start small, add speakers later)

- The different types of audio connections and when to use each
- How to connect a soundbar (the most popular and easiest option)
- How to connect external speakers (bookshelf speakers, stereo systems)
- How to set up a full surround sound system
- How to configure your TV's audio settings
- Troubleshooting common audio problems
- Which cables you need and where to get them
- How to position speakers for best sound quality

**To get started:**

- Your TV (and TV remote)
- External speakers or soundbar (or information about which to buy)

- About 30-60 minutes for setup
- TV user manual (optional but helpful—or find PDF online)

**Understanding Your Options:**


**Option 1: Soundbar (Recommended for Most People)**


**What it is:**

- Long, thin speaker bar (typically 28-50 inches wide)
- Sits below TV on stand, or mounts on wall below/above TV
- Contains multiple speaker drivers (usually 2-5+)
- Some include wireless subwoofer
- Powered (plugs into wall outlet)

**Best for:**

- Most people wanting better TV sound
- Those who want simplicity
- Apartment/condo dwellers (less space needed)
- Budget-conscious buyers ($100-600 for quality options)

**Option 2: Soundbar + Subwoofer**


**What it is:**

- Soundbar (as above)
- Plus separate subwoofer (large speaker for bass)
- Subwoofer usually wireless
- Handles low-frequency sounds (explosions, music bass, rumble)

**Best for:**

- Movie enthusiasts
- Music lovers
- Larger rooms
- Those wanting fuller, richer sound

**Option 3: Powered Bookshelf Speakers**


**What they are:**

- Two separate speakers (left and right)
- Powered (built-in amplifier, plug into wall)
- Typically 6-12 inches tall
- Better sound quality than soundbar for the price
- Requires placement on stands or shelves flanking TV

**Best for:**

- Audiophiles (people who care deeply about sound quality)
- Those with space for separate speakers
- Music listening as well as TV
- People comfortable with slightly more complex setup

**Option 4: Full Surround Sound System**


**What it is:**

- 5.1, 7.1, or more speakers
- Front left, center, right speakers
- Rear surround speakers
- Subwoofer
- AV receiver (to control everything)

**Best for:**

- Home theater enthusiasts
- Dedicated media rooms
- Those wanting cinema experience
- People with budget ($500-3000+)
- Those comfortable with complex setup

**For this guide, we'll focus primarily on soundbars and powered speakers, as these are what most people choose. We'll cover surround sound basics but won't go into extensive detail (that's a whole separate guide).**

## Step 1: Identifying Your TV's Audio Output Options


Before connecting anything, you need to know which audio connections your TV has. Let's find them.


**Locating Your TV's Ports:**


**Where to look:**


**Most common locations:**

1. **Back of TV (most ports here):**
    - Lower-right side as you face the TV's back
    - Or centered on back panel
    - May be in recessed area
2. **Side panel:**
    - Left or right side
    - Usually covered by plastic flap
    - May have some audio/video ports
3. **Bottom edge:**
    - Less common
    - Usually just power connection

**How to see them:**

1. **Lean TV forward gently** (if on stand)
    - Have someone help if TV is large
    - Just enough to see back panel
    - Don't tip too far
2. **Use flashlight or phone light**
    - Back panels are often dark
    - Small labels hard to read without light
3. **Take a photo** with phone
    - Can zoom in to read labels
    - Reference later when connecting

**The Audio Output Ports You're Looking For:**


Let's identify each type and understand what they're for.


**Port 1: HDMI ARC or eARC (Best Option - Most Common)**


**What it looks like:**

- Standard HDMI port (small rectangular port)
- Usually labeled "HDMI ARC" or "HDMI 2 (ARC)" or "HDMI eARC"
- Sometimes labeled "Audio Return Channel"
- Often a different color or specially marked

**Why it's the best:**

- Highest audio quality
- Carries audio back from TV to soundbar
- Allows TV remote to control soundbar volume (very convenient)
- Single cable connection
- Supports advanced audio formats (Dolby Atmos, etc.)

**eARC vs ARC:**

- **eARC** (Enhanced Audio Return Channel): Newer, better, higher quality
- **ARC** (Audio Return Channel): Older, still very good
- Both work excellently for most users
- eARC supports higher-quality audio formats

**Port 2: Optical Audio (Digital Optical, TOSLINK)**


**What it looks like:**

- Small, pentagon-shaped port
- Usually has a little door/flap covering it
- May be labeled "Optical," "Digital Audio Out," "TOSLINK," or "S/PDIF"
- Light might shine from inside when TV is on

**Why it's good:**

- Digital audio (high quality)
- Very common (most TVs have it)
- Easy to connect
- Reliable connection

**Why it's second choice:**

- Doesn't allow TV remote to control speaker volume (you need soundbar remote)
- Doesn't support newest audio formats
- Requires separate cable from HDMI

**Port 3: 3.5mm Headphone Jack**


**What it looks like:**

- Same as headphone jack on phone or old MP3 player
- Usually labeled with headphone icon (🎧)
- May be labeled "Audio Out" or "Headphone"
- 1/8 inch circular jack

**Why it's okay:**

- Universal (every soundbar accepts it)
- Simple connection
- Works when nothing else does

**Why it's last choice:**

- Analog audio (lower quality than digital)
- May need adapter cable
- Disables TV's built-in speakers (can't use both)

**Port 4: RCA Audio Outputs (Red and White)**


**What they look like:**

- Two circular ports side-by-side
- One RED, one WHITE
- May be labeled "Audio Out" or "L" (left - white) and "R" (right - red)
- Same as old stereo equipment from 1980s-90s

**Why it's available:**

- Legacy support (for older equipment)
- Very reliable
- Simple to understand

**Why it's not preferred:**

- Analog audio (lower quality)
- Less common on newer TVs
- Bulkier cables

**Port 5: Coaxial Digital Audio**


**What it looks like:**

- Single circular port (orange usually)
- Looks like RCA but is orange-colored
- May be labeled "Coax," "Digital Audio Out," or "S/PDIF"

**Why it exists:**

- Digital audio (good quality)
- Similar to optical but uses different cable

**Why it's rare:**

- Less common than optical
- Most devices use optical or HDMI instead
- Functionally similar to optical

**Checking What Your TV Has:**


**Make a checklist:**


Look at your TV's back panel and check which you have:

- [ ] HDMI ARC or eARC (which port number? ___)
- [ ] Optical audio output
- [ ] 3.5mm headphone jack
- [ ] RCA audio outputs (red/white)
- [ ] Coaxial digital audio
- [ ] None of the above (very unlikely—double-check)

**Connection Priority (Best to Acceptable):**

1. **HDMI ARC/eARC** - Use this if you have it
2. **Optical** - Use if no HDMI ARC
3. **RCA** - Use if no HDMI or Optical
4. **3.5mm headphone jack** - Use as last resort

**Special Case: No Audio Outputs**


**Very old or very cheap TVs might not have audio outputs.**


**Solution:**

- Use HDMI from source devices instead
- Connect cable box, Roku, PlayStation directly to soundbar
- Soundbar passes video to TV (HDMI passthrough)
- Audio plays through soundbar
- We'll cover this in troubleshooting

**Understanding Your Soundbar's Inputs:**


**Now check what your soundbar accepts:**


**Common soundbar inputs:**

- **HDMI (ARC/eARC)** - Usually labeled "HDMI ARC" or "HDMI TV"
- **Optical** - Pentagon-shaped port
- **3.5mm AUX** - Headphone jack style
- **RCA** - Red and white ports
- **Bluetooth** - Wireless (no port, just pairing)

**Your soundbar should have at least 2-3 of these.**


**Matching TV Output to Soundbar Input:**


**Ideal scenario:**

- TV has HDMI ARC
- Soundbar has HDMI ARC
- Use HDMI cable to connect

**Alternative scenario:**

- TV has Optical
- Soundbar has Optical
- Use optical cable

**You want to use the highest-quality connection both devices share.**


**If devices don't share a common connection:**

- May need adapter or converter
- Example: TV has only headphone jack, soundbar has only optical
- Need headphone-to-optical converter (available on Amazon, $15-30)

**Finding Your TV's Model Number:**


**If you need to look up specifications:**


**Where to find model number:**

1. **Back of TV** - Sticker with model info
2. **Original box or manual**
3. **TV settings menu** - Settings > Support > About This TV

**Model number format examples:**

- Samsung: UN55TU8000 or QN65Q80T
- LG: OLED55C1PUB or 65UN7300
- Sony: XBR-55X900H
- Vizio: M55Q7-J01

**Looking up specifications:**

1. Google: "[Your TV model number] specifications"
2. Find manufacturer's official spec page
3. Look for "Audio" or "Connectivity" section
4. See what audio outputs are listed

**Common TV Brands and Their Audio Outputs:**


**Samsung (2018+):**

- HDMI ARC (older models)
- HDMI eARC (2020+)
- Optical
- Sometimes Bluetooth output

**LG (2018+):**

- HDMI ARC or eARC
- Optical
- Bluetooth

**Sony (2018+):**

- HDMI ARC or eARC
- Optical
- Headphone jack

**Vizio:**

- HDMI ARC
- Optical
- Often RCA and headphone jack

**TCL/Hisense (budget brands):**

- HDMI ARC
- Optical
- Headphone jack
- Sometimes RCA

**Most modern TVs (2016+) have at least HDMI ARC and Optical. If your TV is older than 2016, it likely has Optical and possibly RCA.**


**Questions to Answer Before Proceeding:**


Before moving to the connection steps, confirm:

1. **What audio outputs does my TV have?** _______________
2. **Which one will I use?** _______________
3. **Does my soundbar have matching input?** _______________
4. **Do I have the right cable?** _______________

**If you answered all four questions, you're ready to connect. If not, keep reading to understand which cable you need.**


**The HDMI ARC Sweet Spot:** If both your TV and soundbar have HDMI ARC, you're in luck—this is the easiest and best option. One cable, high quality audio, and your TV remote controls the soundbar volume. This is what we'll cover first and most thoroughly. If you don't have HDMI ARC, don't worry—optical is nearly as good, and we'll cover that too.


## Step 2: Getting the Right Cables


Based on what connections you've identified, you need the appropriate cable. Let's figure out exactly what you need.


**Cable Type 1: HDMI Cable (for HDMI ARC/eARC)**


**What you need:**

- Standard HDMI cable
- **High-Speed HDMI** or **HDMI 2.0** (supports ARC)
- **HDMI 2.1** (supports eARC - better for newer TVs)
- **Length:** 3-6 feet is typical

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy
- $8-15 for quality cable

**Recommendations:**

- **Budget:** AmazonBasics High-Speed HDMI ($8)
- **Quality:** Monoprice Certified Premium ($12)
- **Don't overspend:** Expensive "premium" cables ($50+) offer no benefit for ARC

**Important notes:**

- **Any High-Speed HDMI cable works for ARC**
- You don't need expensive cables
- HDMI is digital (either it works or it doesn't)
- Monster cables ($100) work exactly the same as $10 cables for ARC

**You might already have this:**

- Check cables from cable box, Blu-ray player, game console
- If you have spare HDMI cable, try it first

**Cable Type 2: Optical Audio Cable (TOSLINK, Digital Optical)**


**What it looks like:**

- Black cable with square plastic ends
- Ends have removable plastic caps (protect the optical connector)
- Light fiber inside (don't bend too sharply)

**What you need:**

- TOSLINK optical cable
- **Length:** 3-6 feet typical
- Longer available if needed (up to 30 feet)

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy
- $8-12 for quality cable

**Recommendations:**

- **Budget:** AmazonBasics Digital Optical ($8)
- **Quality:** Monoprice TOSLINK ($10)

**Important notes:**

- Remove plastic caps from both ends before connecting
- Don't bend cable too sharply (fiber inside can break)
- Clean connectors if dusty (use soft cloth)

**Sometimes included:**

- Many soundbars include optical cable in box
- Check soundbar packaging before buying

**Cable Type 3: 3.5mm to 3.5mm (Aux Cable)**


**What it looks like:**

- Like headphone cable
- 3.5mm plug on each end
- Usually black, sometimes red/white

**What you need:**

- 3.5mm stereo audio cable (male to male)
- **Length:** 3-6 feet

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon, Walmart, electronics stores
- $5-8

**Recommendation:**

- AmazonBasics 3.5mm Male to Male Stereo Audio Cable ($6)

**Important notes:**

- Make sure it's stereo (two black rings on plug, not one)
- Cheap but works fine (no need for expensive version)

**Cable Type 4: 3.5mm to RCA (if needed)**


**When you need this:**

- TV has headphone jack (3.5mm)
- Soundbar has RCA inputs (red/white)

**What it looks like:**

- 3.5mm plug on one end
- Red and white RCA plugs on other end

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon, electronics stores
- $8-12

**Cable Type 5: RCA Audio Cable (Red/White)**


**What it looks like:**

- Two cables bundled together
- Red plug and white plug on each end
- Sometimes yellow (video) included—you don't need yellow

**What you need:**

- RCA stereo audio cable (2-channel)
- **Length:** 3-6 feet

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon, Walmart
- $7-10

**Note:** You only need red and white for audio. Yellow is for video (not needed).


**Cable Type 6: RCA to 3.5mm (if needed)**


**When you need this:**

- TV has RCA outputs (red/white)
- Soundbar has 3.5mm input

**What it looks like:**

- RCA red and white on one end
- 3.5mm stereo plug on other end

**Where to buy:**

- Amazon
- $8-10

**Quick Reference Chart:**


| TV Output         | Soundbar Input | Cable Needed         |
| ----------------- | -------------- | -------------------- |
| HDMI ARC          | HDMI ARC       | HDMI cable           |
| Optical           | Optical        | Optical cable        |
| Headphone (3.5mm) | AUX (3.5mm)    | 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable |
| Headphone (3.5mm) | RCA            | 3.5mm to RCA cable   |
| RCA (red/white)   | RCA            | RCA audio cable      |
| RCA               | AUX (3.5mm)    | RCA to 3.5mm cable   |


**Cable Shopping Tips:**


**What matters:**

1. **Correct connector types** (matches your devices)
2. **Right length** (measure the distance)
3. **Decent quality** (Amazon Basics, Monoprice are fine)

**What doesn't matter:**

1. **Premium branding** (waste of money)
2. **Gold plating** (negligible benefit)
3. **Oxygen-free copper** (marketing hype for digital cables)
4. **Monster/AudioQuest premium cables** ($50-200 cables don't sound better)

**For HDMI and Optical (digital signals): Cheap cables work identically to expensive ones.**


**Cable Length Considerations:**


**How to measure:**

1. Measure distance from TV's output port to where soundbar will sit
2. Add 1-2 feet extra (for routing behind furniture, not pulling tight)
3. Round up to nearest standard length (3ft, 6ft, 10ft, 15ft)

**Example:**

- TV to soundbar: 4 feet
- Add slack: +2 feet = 6 feet
- Buy: 6-foot cable

**Common lengths available:**

- 3 feet (1m)
- 6 feet (2m)
- 10 feet (3m)
- 15 feet (5m)
- 25 feet (8m) - for wall-mounted equipment

**Too short:** Won't reach, cable pulls tight (bad)
**Too long:** Extra cable to manage, but not a problem (just coil excess neatly behind TV)


**Better to have slightly too long than too short.**


**Checking What Came With Your Soundbar:**


**Most soundbars include:**

- Power cable (definitely)
- Optical cable (often)
- Sometimes HDMI cable
- Sometimes 3.5mm cable

**Check the box before buying cables:**

1. Look in soundbar packaging
2. Check included accessories
3. Identify which cables came with it

**Read the manual:**

- "What's in the box" section
- Lists included cables

**You might already have everything you need.**


**If You Need to Buy Cables:**


**Best places to buy:**


**Amazon:**

- Widest selection
- User reviews helpful
- 1-2 day shipping (Prime)
- Easy returns

**Walmart/Target:**

- In-store pickup available
- Comparable prices
- Can buy and use same day

**Best Buy:**

- In-store experts can help identify
- Slightly more expensive
- Same-day purchase

**Monoprice.com:**

- Best prices for quality cables
- Shipping takes 3-5 days
- Great if you're ordering in advance

**Where NOT to buy:**

- Airport kiosks (extremely overpriced)
- Gas stations (poor quality, overpriced)
- Convenience stores (limited selection, expensive)

**Cable Buying Checklist:**


Before purchasing, confirm:

- [ ] I know which connection type I'm using (HDMI/Optical/RCA/etc.)
- [ ] I've measured the distance I need
- [ ] I've checked what came with my soundbar
- [ ] I've confirmed the cable I'm buying has correct connectors on BOTH ends
- [ ] I'm not overspending on "premium" features I don't need

**Cable Adapters (When Devices Don't Match):**


**Sometimes you need an adapter:**


**Common scenarios:**


**TV has only headphone jack, soundbar has only optical:**

- Need: Headphone to Optical Converter
- Example: Prozor 192KHz DAC Converter ($20-30)
- Converts analog to digital

**TV has only RCA, soundbar has only optical:**

- Need: RCA to Optical Converter
- Example: Neoteck Aluminum RCA to Digital Converter ($20)

**These adapters are available on Amazon, usually $15-30.**


**Now that you know which cable you need, let's move on to actually making the connection!**


**The Cable Industry's Dirty Secret:** Electronics stores make huge profits on expensive cables by convincing people that gold-plated, oxygen-free, premium cables provide better audio or video quality. For digital signals (HDMI, optical), this is false. A $10 cable transmits the exact same 1s and 0s as a $100 cable. Save your money—buy budget cables from Amazon or Monoprice and spend the savings on a better soundbar.


## Step 3: Connecting a Soundbar Using HDMI ARC


Let's connect your soundbar using HDMI ARC—the best and easiest method.


**What You'll Need:**

- TV
- Soundbar
- HDMI cable
- Both devices plugged into power (but can be off for now)
- TV remote
- Soundbar remote (if it came with one)

**Physical Setup First:**


**Step 1: Position the soundbar**


**If soundbar goes below TV (most common):**

1. **Place soundbar on TV stand** directly in front of TV
2. **Center it** relative to TV
3. **Leave small gap** between soundbar and TV edge (1-2 inches if possible)
4. **Make sure soundbar doesn't block TV's infrared sensor**
    - IR sensor is where remote signal is received
    - Usually bottom-center of TV
    - Point remote at TV—if soundbar blocks signal, TV won't respond to remote
    - Move soundbar forward slightly if needed

**If wall-mounting soundbar:**

- Mount below TV (most common)
- Or above TV (less common but works)
- Use included wall mount brackets
- Center it with TV
- Follow soundbar's mounting instructions

**Step 2: Plug in soundbar power**

1. **Find soundbar's power cord**
2. **Plug into soundbar** (power port usually on back)
3. **Plug into wall outlet or power strip**
4. **Note:** Some soundbars have external power adapter (brick), some have direct cord

**Step 3: If soundbar has separate subwoofer**


**For wireless subwoofer (most common):**

1. **Place subwoofer** somewhere in room
    - Doesn't have to be near TV
    - Corner placement often enhances bass
    - Experiment with placement for best sound
2. **Plug subwoofer into power**
3. **Turn on soundbar**
4. **Subwoofer should pair automatically**
    - Light on subwoofer indicates pairing
    - Check soundbar manual for pairing button if not automatic

**For wired subwoofer:**

1. **Connect cable** from soundbar to subwoofer
2. **Place subwoofer** near TV (cable limits placement)
3. **Plug subwoofer into power**

**Making the HDMI ARC Connection:**


**Step 1: Locate HDMI ARC port on TV**

1. **Look at back of TV** (use flashlight)
2. **Find HDMI port labeled "ARC" or "eARC"**
    - Usually HDMI 1 or HDMI 2
    - Check all HDMI ports for ARC label
    - May be marked with different color or icon

**If you can't find it:**

- Check TV manual
- Google: "[Your TV model] which HDMI port is ARC"
- All HDMI ports might look the same, but only one supports ARC

**Step 2: Locate HDMI ARC port on soundbar**

1. **Look at back of soundbar**
2. **Find port labeled "HDMI ARC," "HDMI (ARC)," or "HDMI OUT (TV)"**
    - Soundbars usually have only one HDMI ARC port
    - Different from HDMI IN ports (which are for source devices)

**Step 3: Connect HDMI cable**

1. **Take HDMI cable**
2. **Remove any protective caps** from cable ends
3. **Insert one end into TV's HDMI ARC port**
    - HDMI only fits one way
    - Don't force—if it doesn't go in easily, try rotating 180°
    - Push until firmly seated (you'll feel it click)
4. **Insert other end into soundbar's HDMI ARC port**
    - Same process—insert gently until seated

**Visual check:**

- Cable is firmly inserted at both ends
- Neither end is loose
- Cable is not bent at sharp angle at connectors

**Step 4: Turn everything on**

1. **Turn on TV** (using TV remote)
2. **Turn on soundbar** (power button on soundbar or remote)
3. **Check if soundbar lights up** (indicates it's receiving power and on)

**Configuring TV Settings for HDMI ARC:**


**Now we need to tell your TV to send audio through HDMI ARC.**


**Step 1: Access TV audio settings**


**Samsung TV:**

1. Press **Home** button
2. Settings (gear icon)
3. **Sound** or **Sound Output**
4. Select **Sound Output**
5. Choose **HDMI ARC** or **Receiver (HDMI ARC)**

**LG TV:**

1. Press **Settings** button (gear icon on remote)
2. **All Settings**
3. **Sound**
4. **Sound Out**
5. Select **HDMI ARC**

**Sony TV:**

1. Press **Home**
2. **Settings**
3. **Sound** or **Display & Sound**
4. **Audio Output**
5. Select **Audio System** or **HDMI ARC**

**Vizio TV:**

1. Press **Menu**
2. **Audio**
3. **Audio Output**
4. Select **HDMI ARC**

**TCL/Roku TV:**

1. Press **Home** (Roku button)
2. **Settings**
3. **Audio**
4. **Audio Output**
5. Select **HDMI ARC** or **AVR**

**Generic steps if your brand isn't listed:**

1. Press Settings or Menu
2. Look for Sound, Audio, or Audio Settings
3. Find Audio Output or Sound Output
4. Select HDMI ARC, Audio System, or External Speaker

**Step 2: Enable HDMI-CEC (important for TV remote control)**


**HDMI-CEC** allows your TV remote to control soundbar volume. Different brands call it different things:


**Samsung:** Anynet+ (HDMI-CEC)
**LG:** SimpLink
**Sony:** Bravia Sync
**Vizio:** CEC
**Roku TV:** 1-touch play or System audio control


**How to enable:**


**Samsung:**

1. Settings > General
2. **External Device Manager**
3. **Anynet+ (HDMI-CEC)** > Turn **On**

**LG:**

1. Settings > General
2. **HDMI Settings**
3. **SimpLink (HDMI-CEC)** > Turn **On**

**Sony:**

1. Settings > Watching TV
2. **External Inputs**
3. **Bravia Sync Settings**
4. **HDMI Device Control** > Turn **On**

**Vizio:**

1. Settings > System
2. **CEC** > Turn **On**

**Roku TV:**

1. Settings > System
2. **Control other devices (CEC)**
3. **System audio control** > Enable
4. **1-touch play** > Enable

**What enabling CEC does:**

- TV remote controls soundbar volume
- Turning on TV can turn on soundbar automatically
- Turning off TV turns off soundbar
- Much more convenient—one remote controls everything

**Step 3: Test the connection**

1. **Play something on TV** (any channel, app, or streaming service)
2. **Listen for audio from soundbar** (not TV speakers)
3. **Check soundbar lights** (should indicate active input)
4. **Use TV remote to adjust volume**
    - Volume should change on soundbar
    - TV should show soundbar is controlling audio

**If you hear audio from soundbar: Success! Connection is complete.**


**If you don't hear audio, proceed to troubleshooting below.**


**Troubleshooting HDMI ARC Connection:**


**Problem: No sound from soundbar**


**Solution 1: Check input selection on soundbar**

- Soundbar must be on HDMI ARC input
- Press "Input" or "Source" button on soundbar remote
- Cycle through inputs until you see "HDMI ARC" or "TV" or "ARC"
- Each press cycles to different input (HDMI, Optical, Bluetooth, AUX)

**Solution 2: Check cables**

- Make sure HDMI cable is firmly seated at both ends
- Try unplugging and re-plugging both ends
- Try a different HDMI cable if you have one

**Solution 3: Power cycle everything**

1. Turn off TV and soundbar
2. Unplug both from power
3. Wait 30 seconds
4. Plug back in
5. Turn on soundbar first, then TV

**Solution 4: Check TV settings again**

- Confirm Audio Output is set to HDMI ARC (not TV Speaker)
- Confirm HDMI-CEC is enabled
- Some TVs require both settings

**Solution 5: Update TV firmware**

- Settings > Support > Software Update (Samsung)
- Older firmware sometimes has HDMI ARC bugs
- Update to latest version

**Problem: Sound from soundbar but TV remote doesn't control volume**


**Solution: Enable HDMI-CEC**

- Follow CEC instructions above
- Make sure it's turned ON
- Might be called Anynet+, SimpLink, Bravia Sync, etc. (see brand names above)

**Problem: Audio cuts out intermittently**


**Solution 1: Check HDMI cable quality**

- Try different HDMI cable
- Make sure using High-Speed HDMI rated cable

**Solution 2: Check HDMI-CEC settings**

- Too many CEC devices can cause conflicts
- Try disabling CEC on other HDMI devices

**Solution 3: Disable eARC (use regular ARC instead)**

- Some TV/soundbar combinations have eARC compatibility issues
- Settings > Sound > HDMI eARC > Disable
- Use regular ARC instead

**Problem: Sound is out of sync with video (lip sync issue)**


**Solution:**

1. Settings > Sound > Audio Delay or AV Sync
2. Adjust delay until audio matches video
3. Usually 50-200ms adjustment needed
4. Or check soundbar manual for lip sync adjustment

**Advanced HDMI ARC Settings:**


**Audio Format (may need to adjust):**


**If using basic soundbar:**

- Set to **PCM** or **Stereo**
- Settings > Sound > Audio Format > PCM

**If using premium soundbar (Dolby Atmos capable):**

- Set to **Auto** or **Bitstream** or **Dolby Digital**
- Allows soundbar to receive and decode surround sound formats

**Most soundbars work fine with default settings.**


**Final Steps:**

1. **Organize cables neatly**
    - Route behind TV stand
    - Use cable ties or clips
    - Keep off floor if possible
2. **Test with different content**
    - Watch TV show (check dialogue)
    - Watch movie (check sound effects)
    - Listen to music (check quality)
3. **Adjust soundbar settings**
    - Many soundbars have dialogue enhancement mode
    - Night mode (reduces volume differences)
    - Bass/treble adjustments
    - Explore soundbar's remote/settings
4. **Set comfortable volume level**
    - TV remote now controls soundbar
    - Find comfortable default level
    - Soundbars can get much louder than TV speakers—start low

**You're done! Your soundbar is connected via HDMI ARC and working.**


**The Remote Control Magic:** The best part about HDMI ARC isn't just the audio quality—it's the convenience. Once HDMI-CEC is enabled, your TV remote becomes your only remote. Volume up/down adjusts the soundbar, mute works, and often turning the TV off will shut down the soundbar too. No more juggling two remotes or looking for the soundbar remote. This is why HDMI ARC is the gold standard for soundbar connections.


## Step 4: Connecting a Soundbar Using Optical Cable


If your TV doesn't have HDMI ARC, or you're having issues with it, optical is your next best option.


**What You'll Need:**

- TV
- Soundbar
- Optical audio cable (TOSLINK)
- Both devices plugged in
- TV remote
- Soundbar remote

**Physical Setup (Same as HDMI ARC):**


**Position soundbar:** (See Step 3 for details)

- Below or above TV
- Centered
- Not blocking IR sensor
- Plug into power

**Subwoofer setup:** (If applicable)

- See Step 3 for wireless or wired setup

**Making the Optical Connection:**


**Step 1: Locate optical port on TV**

1. **Look at back of TV** (use flashlight)
2. **Find optical audio output**
    - Small, pentagon-shaped port
    - Often has little door/flap covering it
    - Labeled "Optical," "Digital Audio Out," "Optical Out," or "TOSLINK"
    - May have red light glowing inside (when TV is on)
3. **Open the protective door** (if present)
    - Small flap that swings open
    - Gently push or slide to open

**Step 2: Locate optical port on soundbar**

1. **Look at back of soundbar**
2. **Find optical input**
    - Same pentagon shape
    - Labeled "Optical," "Optical In," "Digital In," or "TOSLINK"
    - May also have protective door

**Step 3: Prepare optical cable**

1. **Remove red plastic caps** from both ends of cable
    - Caps protect optical connectors
    - Pull off gently
    - Keep caps in case you need to store cable later
2. **Inspect cable ends**
    - Should see shiny fiber optic tip
    - Don't touch the tip (fingerprints reduce signal)
    - If dusty, wipe gently with soft cloth

**Step 4: Connect optical cable**

1. **Insert one end into TV's optical port**
    - Pentagon shape only fits one way
    - Align carefully
    - Push gently until it clicks or seats fully
    - Don't force—if it doesn't fit, try rotating slightly
2. **Insert other end into soundbar's optical port**
    - Same process
    - Gentle push until seated
3. **Check connection**
    - Cable should be firmly in both ports
    - When TV is on, you might see red light through cable (this is normal)
    - Cable should not be bent sharply (damages fiber inside)

**Configuring TV Settings for Optical Audio:**


**Step 1: Change TV audio output to Optical**


**Samsung TV:**

1. Press **Home** > Settings
2. **Sound**
3. **Sound Output**
4. Select **Optical** or **Digital Audio Out**

**LG TV:**

1. Settings > All Settings
2. **Sound**
3. **Sound Out**
4. Select **Optical** or **External Speaker (Optical)**

**Sony TV:**

1. Home > Settings
2. **Sound**
3. **Audio Output**
4. Select **Digital Audio Out (Optical)**

**Vizio TV:**

1. Menu > Audio
2. **Audio Output**
3. Select **Optical** or **Bitstream**

**TCL/Roku TV:**

1. Settings > Audio
2. **Audio Output**
3. Select **Optical** or **S/PDIF and ARC**

**Step 2: Configure audio format**


**Most TVs have audio format options for optical:**


**Common settings:**

- **PCM** or **Stereo** (basic, works with all soundbars)
- **Dolby Digital** (if your soundbar supports it)
- **Bitstream** (passes through advanced audio formats)

**For basic soundbar:**

- Choose **PCM** or **Stereo**

**For premium soundbar (Dolby Digital capable):**

- Choose **Dolby Digital** or **Bitstream**

**If unsure, start with PCM and upgrade to Dolby Digital if soundbar supports it.**


**Where to find this setting:**


**Samsung:**

- Settings > Sound > Expert Settings > Digital Audio Format
- Choose PCM or Dolby Digital

**LG:**

- Settings > Sound > Sound Out > Optical Settings
- Choose PCM or Auto (Dolby Digital)

**Sony:**

- Settings > Sound > Audio Output > Digital Audio Out
- Choose PCM or Dolby Digital

**Step 3: Turn off TV speakers (optional but recommended)**


**Some TVs can play audio through both TV speakers and optical simultaneously. This creates echo effect—not desirable.**


**To disable TV speakers:**

- Settings > Sound > TV Speaker > Off
- Or this may happen automatically when you select Optical output

**Testing the Connection:**


**Step 1: Select optical input on soundbar**

1. **Turn on soundbar**
2. **Press "Input" or "Source" button** on soundbar or remote
3. **Cycle through inputs** until you see "Optical," "Digital," or "OPT"
4. **Soundbar should show it's on optical input** (LED display or light indicator)

**Step 2: Play audio on TV**

1. **Turn on TV**
2. **Play something** (any channel, Netflix, etc.)
3. **Listen for audio from soundbar**
4. **Audio should come from soundbar, not TV**

**Step 3: Adjust volume**

1. **Use soundbar remote** to change volume
    - Note: TV remote won't control soundbar volume with optical (unlike HDMI ARC)
    - You need two remotes: TV remote for changing channels, soundbar remote for volume
2. **Set comfortable volume level**

**If audio is working: Success! You're done.**


**Troubleshooting Optical Connection:**


**Problem: No sound from soundbar**


**Solution 1: Check soundbar input**

- Make sure soundbar is set to Optical input
- Press Input/Source button to cycle through
- Look for "Optical" or "Digital" or "OPT" on soundbar display

**Solution 2: Check optical cable connection**

- Make sure both ends are fully inserted
- Check that protective caps are removed
- Look for red light coming from TV's optical port (indicates signal)
- Try reseating both ends

**Solution 3: Check TV audio settings**

- Confirm Audio Output is set to Optical
- Confirm TV speakers are off
- Try changing Digital Audio Format to PCM

**Solution 4: Try different optical cable**

- Cable may be damaged (fiber broken inside)
- Try new optical cable if you have one

**Problem: Sound from soundbar but poor quality or dropouts**


**Solution 1: Check for sharp bends in cable**

- Optical cable shouldn't be bent sharply (damages fiber)
- Smooth out any kinks
- Don't fold or twist cable

**Solution 2: Clean optical connectors**

- Dust on tips reduces signal
- Gently wipe with soft, lint-free cloth
- Don't touch tips with fingers

**Solution 3: Change audio format**

- If set to Dolby Digital, try PCM
- Some soundbars have issues with certain formats
- PCM is most compatible

**Problem: Can't control soundbar volume with TV remote**


**This is normal with optical connection.**


**Optical doesn't support remote control functionality** (unlike HDMI ARC).


**Workarounds:**


**Option 1: Use soundbar remote**

- Keep both remotes handy
- TV remote: channels, apps
- Soundbar remote: volume

**Option 2: Universal remote**

- Program universal remote to control both TV and soundbar
- Logitech Harmony remotes work well ($50-250)
- One remote controls both devices

**Option 3: Get a soundbar with learning remote**

- Some soundbars can "learn" TV remote commands
- Program soundbar to respond to your TV remote
- Check soundbar manual for this feature

**Option 4: Switch to HDMI ARC if possible**

- Provides remote control functionality
- See Step 3

**Advantages of Optical vs HDMI ARC:**


**Optical pros:**

- ✓ Works on older TVs without HDMI ARC
- ✓ Very reliable connection
- ✓ No compatibility issues
- ✓ Immune to HDMI handshake problems

**Optical cons:**

- ✗ Can't control soundbar with TV remote
- ✗ Doesn't support newest audio formats (Dolby Atmos, etc.)
- ✗ Requires separate cable

**For most people, optical provides excellent audio quality that's indistinguishable from HDMI ARC for regular TV watching.**


**Optical Cable Care:**


**Do:**

- ✓ Route cable gently without sharp bends
- ✓ Keep protective caps if you need to disconnect later
- ✓ Avoid stepping on cable
- ✓ Secure with cable ties, but not too tight

**Don't:**

- ✗ Bend cable at sharp right angles
- ✗ Twist or kink cable
- ✗ Pull on cable (remove by grasping connector, not cable)
- ✗ Touch optical tips with fingers

**Final Steps:**

1. **Test with different content**
    - TV shows (dialogue)
    - Movies (sound effects)
    - Music (quality)
2. **Adjust soundbar settings**
    - Dialogue mode
    - Bass/treble
    - Night mode
    - Sound modes (Movie, Music, etc.)
3. **Organize cables**
    - Route optical cable neatly
    - Avoid sharp bends
    - Cable ties for management
4. **Keep soundbar remote accessible**
    - You'll need it for volume
    - Consider a remote caddy or holder

**You're done! Soundbar is connected via optical and working.**

> **Why Two Remotes Isn't the End of the World:** Yes, using optical means you need the soundbar remote for volume control—slightly less convenient than HDMI ARC. But in practice, most people adjust volume rarely once they find a comfortable level. And some soundbars have smartphone apps that can replace the physical remote. The audio quality is excellent, and for older TVs without HDMI ARC, optical is a perfect solution. Don't let the two-remote situation discourage you.
